cards.front: For a survey about Year 12 students in one school, what is the population?
cards.back: Year 12 students in that school.

cards.front: A principal asks every student in a college about a timetable. What method is this?
cards.back: Census.

cards.front: If some groups are systematically more likely to be selected, what problem is present?
cards.back: Bias.

cards.front: A sample is chosen from the [ ___ ] and used to draw conclusions about that larger group.
cards.back: A sample is chosen from the population and used to draw conclusions about that larger group.

cards.front: For a gym surveying active members, what is a suitable sampling frame?
cards.back: An up-to-date list of active members.

cards.front: In a sports centre membership database, what are the sampling units?
cards.back: The individual members.

cards.front: A sampling frame should match the [ ___ ] as closely as possible.
cards.back: A sampling frame should match the population as closely as possible.

cards.front: A computer selects donor numbers at random from a list. What sampling method is this?
cards.back: Simple random sampling.

cards.front: In simple random sampling, every member has an [ ___ ] of being selected.
cards.back: In simple random sampling, every member has an equal chance of being selected.

cards.front: What must be complete for simple random sampling to be relatively unbiased?
cards.back: The sampling frame.

cards.front: What can still happen by chance in a simple random sample?
cards.back: Some groups may be under-represented.

cards.front: A teacher chooses every 6th name from an ordered list. What sampling method is this?
cards.back: Systematic sampling.

cards.front: Systematic sampling selects at [ ___ ] from an [ ___ ].
cards.back: Systematic sampling selects at regular intervals from an ordered list.

cards.front: When can systematic sampling become biased?
cards.back: When a list pattern or cycle matches the interval.

cards.front: The population is split into groups and proportional numbers are chosen. What method is this?
cards.back: Stratified sampling.

cards.front: In stratified sampling, bigger strata should contribute [ ___ ] than smaller strata.
cards.back: In stratified sampling, bigger strata should contribute more people than smaller strata.

cards.front: For stratified sampling: number from stratum = [ ___ ] ÷ population size × [ ___ ].
cards.back: For stratified sampling: number from stratum = stratum size ÷ population size × sample size.

cards.front: A school has 640 pupils, 72 in a stratum, and wants a sample of 50. How many from that stratum?
A student asks pupils until he has 20 boys and 20 girls. What sampling method is this?
cards.back: Quota sampling.

cards.front: Quota sampling fills [ ___ ] from groups, usually without [ ___ ] selection.
cards.back: Quota sampling fills fixed numbers from groups, usually without random selection.

cards.front: Why can quota sampling be biased?
cards.back: The researcher may choose convenient people.

cards.front: A manager asks the first 30 gym members entering on Tuesday morning. What method is this?
cards.back: Opportunity sampling.

cards.front: Opportunity sampling is also called [ ___ ].
cards.back: Opportunity sampling is also called convenience sampling.

cards.front: Why may opportunity sampling fail to represent the population?
cards.back: It only uses people easiest to reach.
